title: The Argument You Can't Afford to Win
author: Greg McKeown
summary: In this 1-Minute Wednesday, Greg McKeown reflects on a respectful disagreement with a friend that ended with neither convinced, and realizes he had measured success by persuasion when he should have measured it by understanding. He cites a 2025 study by Guy Itzchakov and colleagues, covering nearly 1,400 people, in which good listening made participants more open to opposing perspectives without changing their attitudes toward the opposing group. For leaders, he says making agreement the goal of communication risks cutting off the people who tell you what they see, giving agreement just when you most need perspective. The same holds in marriages and families, where hard subjects must be revisited without risking the relationship. He closes with a four-step practice for reaching an Exactly: restate their view, ask what you got wrong, listen, and try again.
points: McKeown realized he had been measuring a disagreement by persuasion rather than by understanding.
A 2025 study found that feeling listened to made people more open to opposing views without making them more agreeable.
He warns leaders that aiming for agreement can stop dissenters from telling you what they see.
He applies the same logic to spouses, children and close friends, where the goal is to keep talking.
He offers a four-step practice, ending when you can state the other person's point to their satisfaction.
quotes: I had been defining success on persuasion and agreement, when I should have been measuring it on understanding.
As a leader, making agreement and persuasion your top communication goal has real consequences.
You need people who disagree with you to continue telling you what they see. Otherwise, you may get agreement at the very moment you most need perspective.
But as I evaluated the experience, I noted something important: I didn't feel any further apart from him. In some ways, I felt closer.
And even if we make a brilliant argument, what have we accomplished if the other person becomes less willing to tell us what they think?
We hadn't reached an agreement. But we had made it possible to keep talking.
Listen to their corrections. Try again until you can make their point to their satisfaction.
